presentingComplaint: Cough for 3 months with recent blood-streaked sputum and 8 kg weight loss.
history: A 66-year-old man, 45 pack-year smoker with known alcohol-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, on spironolactone and propranolol for varices), presents with a persistent cough for about 3 months that has changed in character over the last 6 weeks, now productive with intermittent blood-streaked sputum. He reports progressive exertional breathlessness, a dull right-sided chest ache, drenching night sweats and an unintentional weight loss of roughly 8 kg over 2 months, which he and his GP initially attributed to worsening liver disease and poor appetite. He denies contact with tuberculosis and had a negative sputum AFB smear x2 arranged by his GP. He has mild ankle swelling and a distended abdomen he says is 'the usual fluid'. No recent fever spikes. He continues to drink intermittently and has had one prior admission for ascites.
examination: Cachectic, mildly icteric man. Clubbing present. Right supraclavicular lymphadenopathy (1.5 cm, firm, non-tender). Reduced breath sounds and dullness at the right base with reduced expansion. Abdomen distended with shifting dullness (grade 2 ascites) and a firm irregular liver edge; spider naevi and palmar erythema present. No asterixis. No focal neurological deficit.
imaging: Chest radiograph: 4.5 cm spiculated mass in the right upper lobe with right hilar prominence and a small right pleural effusion. CECT thorax/upper abdomen: 4.8 cm spiculated RUL mass invading the mediastinal pleura, enlarged right hilar and subcarinal nodes, right supraclavicular node, and small right malignant-appearing pleural effusion; cirrhotic liver with splenomegaly and ascites, no discrete liver metastasis on this study. Two subcentimetre indeterminate hepatic lesions noted against a nodular cirrhotic background.
microbiology: Sputum AFB smear negative x3; sputum culture and GeneXpert MTB/RIF not detected. Pleural fluid: exudate, lymphocyte-predominant, ADA not elevated, cytology positive for malignant cells.
differentialDiagnoses: Primary lung cancer (non-small-cell) with nodal and pleural spread
Malignant pleural effusion secondary to another primary
Interstitial lung disease with traction changes
finalDiagnosis: Primary lung cancer (right upper lobe mass, likely NSCLC) with hilar/supraclavicular nodal and malignant pleural involvement, on a background of alcohol-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B) complicating the clinical picture and management.
citations: NICE - Lung cancer: diagnosis and management (NG122) - 2019
ACCP/CHEST - Diagnosis and Staging of Lung Cancer - 2013
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e - Neoplasms of the Lung
stewardship: Not applicable - this is a non-infective (neoplastic) presentation. TB has been actively excluded (repeated negative AFB/GeneXpert, pleural ADA not raised, positive malignant cytology), so empiric antitubercular or antibacterial therapy is not indicated and should be withheld. Antimicrobials would only be justified if a secondary infection were later documented.
contraindications: Hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B) and thrombocytopenia/coagulopathy (INR 1.5, platelets 96) increase bleeding risk for transbronchial/CT-guided biopsy - correct coagulopathy and choose safest sampling route (e.g., pleural fluid cytology or supraclavicular node biopsy first).
Avoid hepatotoxic and renally cleared chemotherapy dosing without adjustment; many systemic agents require dose modification in cirrhosis.
Contrast load with caution given cirrhosis-related haemodynamics; avoid nephrotoxic insults.
edgeCases: Weight loss, night sweats and reduced appetite wrongly attributed to decompensating cirrhosis, delaying cancer diagnosis.
Hypercalcaemia (corrected Ca 11.6) as a paraneoplastic feature rather than a primary metabolic disorder.
Thrombocytopenia here is from hypersplenism/cirrhosis, not marrow infiltration - affects biopsy planning.
Small indeterminate hepatic nodules on a cirrhotic background raise the question of HCC versus metastasis, needing dedicated liver imaging.
expectedMaiK: Recognise a spiculated lung mass with nodal, pleural and paraneoplastic features as probable primary lung cancer and prioritise tissue diagnosis by the safest route plus staging, while accounting for cirrhosis-related bleeding risk and treatment limitations.
expectedNextQuestions: Smoking pack-year history and any occupational asbestos exposure?
Timeline and magnitude of weight loss versus known liver disease?
Any bone pain, headache or neurological symptoms suggesting metastasis?
Current performance status and Child-Pugh/decompensation history to gauge fitness for investigation and therapy?
expectedInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT thorax and upper abdomen (staging and mass characterisation)
Tissue diagnosis via least-invasive route (pleural fluid cytology, supraclavicular node FNA/biopsy, or EBUS-TBNA)
PET-CT for metabolic staging and MRI brain if symptomatic
Coagulation profile, platelets and LFTs prior to any biopsy; correct coagulopathy
Dedicated liver imaging (triple-phase CT/MRI) to characterise cirrhotic nodules and AFP
Molecular/PD-L1 testing on tissue once histology confirmed

investigations: Tissue biopsy (pleural cytology / supraclavicular node / EBUS-TBNA)
Coagulation profile and platelets before biopsy
